As at 2026-11-06, section 15 of the Active Mobility Act 2017 generally prohibits riding a bicycle on a pedestrian-only path, subject to two exceptions. [CITE:1]

A cyclist may ride on a pedestrian-only path:

1. **When crossing it:** the cyclist must cross by the shortest safe route and must not remain on the path longer than necessary to cross it safely. [CITE:1]

2. **To avoid an obstruction:** there must be an obstruction on an adjacent road, footpath or shared path; travelling on that adjacent area must be impracticable; and the cyclist must travel no more than reasonably necessary along the pedestrian-only path to avoid the obstruction. [CITE:1]

Even where either exception applies, section 22 separately prohibits riding on any public path recklessly or in a manner dangerous to the public, having regard to all the circumstances; an offence may result in a fine not exceeding $10,000, imprisonment for up to 12 months, or both. [CITE:4]

As at 2026-11-06, on the supplied statutory texts, the short answer is: **using a handheld phone while moving is generally prohibited; using a properly worn smartwatch is generally permitted.** [CITE:1]

- **Handheld phone:** Assuming the e-scooter is a statutory “vehicle” and the footpath is a public path, section 22A of the Active Mobility Act prohibits its rider from holding a phone in the hand and operating any communication or other function while the e-scooter is moving. Covered functions include calls, text and video messages, electronic documents and internet access. [CITE:1]

- **Smart watch:** A smartwatch falls within the broad definition of “mobile communication device,” but section 22A expressly exempts a wearable device when it is worn in the manner intended by its manufacturer. A smartwatch worn and operated as intended is therefore not caught by that specific prohibition. [CITE:1]

- **Phone not held in the hand:** Section 22A requires both hand-holding and operation. Its wording does not prohibit operating a phone that is not being held in the hand. [CITE:1]

- **Other riding offences still apply:** Riding a personal mobility device recklessly or in a manner dangerous to the public on any public path is a separate offence. The statute does not classify every instance of phone or smartwatch use as dangerous, but the manner of riding may independently breach that rule. [CITE:13]

- **Parallel road/public-place rule:** Section 65B of the Road Traffic Act similarly prohibits a driver of a vehicle from holding and operating a mobile communication device while the vehicle is moving on a road or in a public place, while exempting wearables worn as intended by their manufacturer. [CITE:5]

- **Penalties:** A contravention of section 22A is punishable by up to $1,000, up to three months’ imprisonment, or both; the corresponding repeat-offender limits are $2,000 and six months. [CITE:1]

As at 2026-11-06, under the Bills of Lading Act 1992, the principal effect of becoming the lawful holder of a bill of lading is that **all rights of suit under the contract of carriage are transferred to and vested in the holder as if the holder had been a party to that contract**, subject to the statutory conditions. [CITE:1]

For a bill of lading, the “contract of carriage” means the contract contained in or evidenced by that bill. [CITE:4]

The holder may be the consignee identified in the bill who possesses it, a transferee who possesses it following a completed endorsement or, for a bearer bill, its transfer, or a qualifying successor who would have become a holder but for a transaction occurring after possession ceased to give a right against the carrier to possession of the goods. [CITE:4] A person is regarded as having become the lawful holder wherever they became the holder in good faith. [CITE:4]

The Act applies to bills of lading capable of transfer by endorsement or, for a bearer bill, by delivery without endorsement, and includes received-for-shipment bills of lading. [CITE:5]

There is an important qualification: if possession of the bill no longer gives a right against the carrier to possession of the goods, no rights are transferred unless the person became the holder either through a transaction under contractual or other arrangements made before that right ceased, or following another person’s rejection of goods or documents delivered in pursuance of those arrangements. [CITE:1]

Where another person has acquired the rights of suit but a person with an interest in the goods has suffered loss or damage from breach of the carriage contract, the holder of the rights may exercise them for the benefit of the person who suffered the loss, to the same extent as if the rights had vested in that person. [CITE:1]

A qualifying bill of lading also provides the holder with an evidentiary advantage: where it represents that goods were shipped or received for shipment and is signed by the master or a person authorised to sign for the carrier, it is conclusive evidence against the carrier of shipment or receipt for shipment. [CITE:2]

The acquisition of rights also carries corresponding contractual liabilities: a person in whom the rights are vested becomes subject to the same liabilities under the carriage contract as if they had been a party if they take or demand delivery from the carrier, make a claim against the carrier, or had taken or demanded delivery before the rights vested in them. [CITE:3]

As at 2026-11-06, generally no. If the ship is missing and no news of her has been received after a reasonable time, section 58 permits an actual total loss to be presumed. Section 57(2) expressly provides that, in an actual loss, no notice of abandonment need be given. [CITE:1][CITE:10]

Section 62 requires notice where the assured elects to abandon the insured subject matter to the insurer; without notice, the loss can only be treated as a partial loss. [CITE:4]

Accordingly, where the section 58 missing-ship presumption of actual total loss applies, notice of abandonment is unnecessary on that basis. If the matter were instead treated as a constructive total loss based on an abandonment, section 60 requires a reasonable abandonment and section 62 governs the notice requirements. [CITE:8][CITE:4][CITE:1]

As at 2026-11-06, a **constructive total loss** is one of the two forms of total loss, the other being an actual total loss [CITE:3].

Subject to any express provision in the policy, section 60 of the Marine Insurance Act 1906 provides that a constructive total loss exists where the subject-matter insured is reasonably abandoned because:

- its actual total loss appears unavoidable; or
- it could not be preserved from actual total loss without expenditure exceeding its value after that expenditure was incurred [CITE:2].

Section 60 identifies particular cases:

- The assured is deprived of possession of the ship or goods by a peril insured against, and it is unlikely that the ship or goods can be recovered, or the recovery cost would exceed their value when recovered [CITE:2].
- A ship is so damaged by a peril insured against that repairing it would cost more than its value after repair; when assessing repair costs, general-average contributions payable by other interests are not deducted, but future salvage expenses and future general-average contributions if the ship were repaired must be taken into account [CITE:2].
- Goods are so damaged that the cost of repairing them and forwarding them to their destination would exceed their value on arrival [CITE:2].

Where a constructive total loss exists, the assured may either treat it as a partial loss or abandon the subject-matter to the insurer and treat it as if it were an actual total loss [CITE:1]. Unless the policy shows a different intention, insurance against total loss includes both constructive and actual total losses [CITE:3]. In a valued policy, the agreed value is not conclusive for determining whether a constructive total loss has occurred unless the policy provides otherwise [CITE:4].

As at 2026-11-06, under section 79(2) of the Marine Insurance Act 1906, an insurer who pays for a **partial loss**:

- Acquires **no title** to the subject-matter insured or to any part that remains. [CITE:1]
- Becomes **subrogated to the assured’s rights and remedies** concerning the subject-matter insured, measured from the time of the casualty causing the loss. [CITE:1]
- Has that subrogation only **to the extent that the payment has indemnified the assured** under the Act. [CITE:1]

This differs from a payment for a total loss, where the insurer becomes entitled to take over the assured’s interest in whatever remains of the subject-matter insured. [CITE:1]

1. before the application under consideration, two or more Singapore passports issued to the applicant have been lost or stolen; and  
2. for reasons of passport security and integrity, the Controller considers it undesirable to issue another passport. [CITE:1]

Section 25 does not state a time limit within which the two losses must have occurred; it requires only that they occurred before the relevant application. [CITE:1] Where the Controller is aware of a section 25 circumstance, section 19 permits the Controller to refuse a Singapore passport to a citizen by written notice. [CITE:6]

A person aggrieved by a refusal may appeal in writing to the Minister within 14 days after receiving notice, or within such longer period as the Minister allows in exceptional circumstances. The appeal must state its grounds, and the Minister’s decision is final. [CITE:10]

Separately, a passport holder must report the loss, theft or destruction of a Singapore passport to an authorised officer within 14 days after first knowing of it; failure to do so is an offence unless there is a reasonable excuse. For a child, this reporting duty falls on a person with parental responsibility. [CITE:11]

As at 2026-11-06, under section 27(1) of the Passports Act 2007, the Controller must not issue a Singapore passport to a child unless the applicable person consents to the child travelling internationally, or a court order permits the child to travel internationally. [CITE:1]

The applicable consent is from either:

- a person with parental responsibility for the child; or
- where the child is covered by a voluntary care agreement or the specified care or protection order, the Director-General of Social Welfare, a protector, or a care-giver, as authorised under that arrangement or order. [CITE:1]

Alternatively, a court order permitting the child to travel internationally satisfies the statutory requirement without requiring one of the above consents. [CITE:1]

For these provisions, a “child” is someone below 16 years of age. [CITE:7] “Parental responsibility” includes being the child’s parent, being a person with whom the child is to live under a court order, or being entitled to guardianship or custody under written law. [CITE:5]

A registration officer includes the Commissioner of National Registration, the Deputy Commissioner, an Assistant Commissioner, or another person appointed as a registration officer. [CITE:18]

Failing to report the change within the required period is an offence punishable on conviction by a fine not exceeding $5,000, imprisonment not exceeding five years, or both. [CITE:3]

As at 2026-11-06, under the National Registration Act 1965, the **person making the claim bears the burden of proof** of Singapore citizenship by birth; this is stated expressly as the "onus of proving the status of citizenship of Singapore by birth" [CITE:1].

In practical terms:

As at 2026-11-06, for a first offence under section 3(1) of the Computer Misuse Act 1993, a person who knowingly causes a computer to perform a function for the purpose of securing access without authority to any program or data may be fined up to $5,000, imprisoned for up to 2 years, or both. [CITE:1]

If damage is caused as a result of the offence, section 3(2) provides for a fine not exceeding $50,000, imprisonment for a term not exceeding 7 years, or both. [CITE:1]

**As at 2026-11-06, the court can order the convicted offender to pay you compensation for damage to your computer data, and that order does not wipe out the rest of your civil claim — it only reduces the claim by the amount you have already been paid under the order [CITE:1] [CITE:17].**

### 1. Compensation order under the Computer Misuse Act

Section 17(1) of the Computer Misuse Act 1993 ("CMA") provides that the court before which a person is convicted of **any offence under the Act** may order that person to pay a sum fixed by the court as compensation to any other person for any damage caused to that person's computer, program or data by the offence for which the sentence is passed [CITE:1].

The most directly relevant offence for data damage is CMA section 5 (unauthorised modification of computer material), which applies to a person who knowingly does any act causing an unauthorised modification of the contents of any computer, and where damage is caused the offender is liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding $50,000 or imprisonment not exceeding 7 years, or both [CITE:14]. Where the offence involves obtaining access to a "protected computer" under CMA section 11 — for example, a computer used directly for banking and financial services, public utilities, public key infrastructure or public safety — the enhanced penalty of a fine not exceeding $100,000 or imprisonment not exceeding 20 years, or both, applies instead [CITE:11]. Other CMA offences that may be engaged by unauthorised access or obstruction are section 3 (unauthorised access to computer material) and section 7 (unauthorised obstruction of use of a computer) [CITE:6] [CITE:3].

The CMA compensation order is enforceable as a civil debt [CITE:1].

### 2. The Criminal Procedure Code framework for compensation

Under section 359(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 ("CPC"), the court before which an offender is convicted must, after the conviction, decide whether to order the offender to pay compensation to persons injured in respect of body, character or property by the offence for which the offender is sentenced, and damage to property falls within that category [CITE:2]. If the court considers an order appropriate, it must make one [CITE:2]. If it declines to make an order, it must give reasons [CITE:2]. In deciding whether to make an order and how much to order, the court must have regard to the offender's means so far as those means appear or are known to the court [CITE:2]. Any order must specify the amount of compensation to be paid [CITE:2].

Note that the person who would receive compensation under section 359(1) — including a person whose property was damaged — may not appeal against the order or against a decision not to make an order [CITE:17].

Payment of a compensation sum is governed by CPC section 360, under which the court may, before the sum is paid in full, allow and extend time for payment, direct payment by instalments, order attachment of the debtor's property (movable or immovable), direct that any debt owing to the debtor be applied towards the sum, direct imprisonment in default of payment, and direct that money found on a search of the debtor be applied to the sum [CITE:19].

### 3. Whether you can still sue

Yes, but the compensation already paid comes off your claim rather than replacing it [CITE:1] [CITE:17].

- Under CMA section 17(2), a claim for damages sustained by reason of the offence is deemed satisfied to the extent of any amount paid to you under a compensation order, but the order does not affect any right to a civil remedy for recovery of damages beyond the amount of compensation paid [CITE:1].
- Under CPC section 359(4), the same applies to a compensation order made under section 359(1): the order does not affect any right to a civil remedy for damages beyond the amount of compensation paid, and any civil claim for the same injury arising from the offence is deemed satisfied to the extent of the amount paid under the order [CITE:17].

In practical terms, if you recover $5,000 by way of a compensation order and your provable loss is $20,000, the paid $5,000 is treated as satisfying that part of your loss, and the remaining $15,000 remains capable of being pursued in civil proceedings [CITE:1] [CITE:17].

### 4. Limits of the provided sources

The sources supplied do not set out which civil cause of action you would use in the civil suit, any limitation period for it, or the procedural mechanics of giving credit for the compensation already paid; they also do not state whether both a CMA section 17 order and a CPC section 359 order may be made in the same conviction [CITE:1] [CITE:2]. For those points, the current full text on Singapore Statutes Online, or a lawyer, would be the appropriate place to look.

As at 2026-11-06, a **Correction Direction** under section 11 of the Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act 2019 is issued to a person who communicated the subject statement in Singapore and requires that person to communicate a **correction notice** in Singapore, in the specified form and manner, to any specified recipients and by the specified time. [CITE:1]

The correction notice must contain at least one of the following: a statement in the specified terms that the subject statement is false or that the specified material contains a false statement of fact; or a specified statement of fact, or a reference to a specified location where that statement of fact may be found. [CITE:1]

The Correction Direction may also require the correction notice to be communicated in one or more of these ways: in a specified online location; placed in specified proximity to every copy of the false statement or a substantially similar statement communicated in Singapore; or published in the specified manner in a specified newspaper or other printed publication in Singapore. [CITE:1]

“Specified” means specified in the Correction Direction itself. [CITE:1]

A person may be issued a Correction Direction even if they did not know, and had no reason to believe, that the statement was false. [CITE:1]

This statutory Correction Direction is distinct from a **Targeted Correction Direction** or **General Correction Direction** under Part 4 of the Act, which are addressed to internet intermediaries, mass-media providers, telecommunications providers, or other prescribed persons. [CITE:2][CITE:3][CITE:7]

**As at 2026-11-06,** a Stop Communication Direction is a Part 3 Direction issued under section 12 of the Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act 2019 (POFMA) [CITE:1][CITE:3] (the statutory extracts provided are from the 2020 Edition, and note that Singapore Statutes Online should be checked for the latest version) [CITE:1].

## What the Direction can require

Section 12 provides that a Stop Communication Direction may require the person to whom it is issued to do any of the following [CITE:1]:

1. **Stop communicating the subject statement.** The Direction may require the person to stop communicating in Singapore the subject statement by the specified time [CITE:1].

2. **Stop communicating substantially similar statements.** The Direction may also require the person to stop communicating any statement that is substantially similar to the subject statement [CITE:1].

3. **Communicate a correction notice in Singapore.** The Direction may require the person to communicate in Singapore a correction notice in the specified form and manner, to a specified person or description of persons (if any), and by the specified time [CITE:1].

4. **Publish a correction notice in print.** The Direction may require the person to publish a correction notice in the specified manner in a specified newspaper or other printed publication of Singapore [CITE:1].

Items 3 and 4 are alternatives in the wording of the statute, which allows the Direction to require the person to do "one or both" of them [CITE:1].

## Key terms

"Stop communicating" means taking the necessary steps to ensure that the statement is no longer available on or through the internet to end-users in Singapore, including, if necessary, removing the statement from an online location [CITE:1].

"Specified" means specified in the Stop Communication Direction itself [CITE:1].

A "correction notice" is the notice defined for Part 3, which must contain either a statement, in such terms as may be specified, that the subject statement is false or that the specified material contains a false statement of fact, or a specified statement of fact, or a reference to a specified location where that statement of fact may be found, or both [CITE:4].

A "statement" is defined broadly to include any word, abbreviation, initial, number, image, sound, symbol or other representation, or a combination of any of these [CITE:3].

An "online location" includes any website, webpage, chatroom or forum, or any other thing hosted on a computer and capable of being seen, heard or otherwise perceived by means of the internet [CITE:3].

## Limits on who is treated as communicating

A person does not communicate a statement in Singapore merely by doing an act for the purpose of, or incidental to, providing an internet intermediary service, a telecommunication service, a service of giving the public access to the internet, or a computing resource service [CITE:1].

## Scope and operation of the Direction

A Part 3 Direction, which includes a Stop Communication Direction, may be issued to a person whether that person is in or outside Singapore, and may require the person to do an act in or outside Singapore [CITE:2][CITE:3].

The Direction must identify the subject statement in sufficient detail, and must comply with any prescribed form, manner and other requirements [CITE:2].

The Direction remains in effect until it expires, if it has an expiry date, or until it is set aside under section 17 or cancelled under section 19 [CITE:2].

The person to whom the Direction is issued is responsible for the costs of complying with it [CITE:2].

## Conditions for issue and liability for non-compliance

A Minister may instruct the Competent Authority to issue a Part 3 Direction if a false statement of fact has been or is being communicated in Singapore and the Minister is of the opinion that it is in the public interest to issue the Direction [CITE:11].

A Stop Communication Direction may be issued even if the person who communicated the false statement of fact did not know, and had no reason to believe, that the statement was false [CITE:1].

Once a Stop Communication Direction has been issued, the Competent Authority must publish a notice of that fact in the Gazette as soon as possible, and a failure to do so does not invalidate the Direction [CITE:1].

A person to whom a Part 3 Direction is issued and served who, without reasonable excuse, fails to comply, whether in or outside Singapore, commits an offence and is liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding $20,000 or imprisonment for a term not exceeding 12 months or both, if the person is an individual, and to a fine not exceeding $500,000 in any other case [CITE:7].

Where a person fails to comply with a Part 3 Direction, the subject statement is being communicated in Singapore on an online location, and the Minister is satisfied that one or more end-users in Singapore have used or are using the services of an internet access service provider to access that online location, the Minister may direct IMDA to order that provider to take reasonable steps to disable access by end-users in Singapore to the online location, and a provider that does not comply with such an order commits an offence [CITE:14].

## Variation, cancellation and appeal

The Minister who instructed the Competent Authority to issue the Direction may at any time instruct the Competent Authority to vary or cancel it, on the Minister's own initiative or on application by the person to whom it was issued, by serving written notice on that person, and the Direction remains in effect pending any such application [CITE:9].

A person to whom a Part 3 Direction is issued may appeal to the General Division of the High Court, but only after first applying to the Minister to vary or cancel the Direction and having that application refused in whole or in part, and the Direction remains in effect while the appeal is pending unless it is set aside or a stay is ordered [CITE:18].

The issue of a Part 3 Direction does not affect the power of any person, including the Competent Authority or the Government, to take other action under POFMA or any other law in relation to the statement, or the power of the Public Prosecutor to initiate proceedings for an offence [CITE:8].

## Related direction distinguished

A Stop Communication Direction is legally distinct from a Correction Direction under section 11, which is the other type of Part 3 Direction [CITE:3][CITE:4]; a Correction Direction requires the communicator to communicate a correction notice and may require placement of the notice near every copy of the false or substantially similar statement that they communicate in Singapore, or publication of the notice in a specified Singapore newspaper or other printed publication [CITE:4].

As at 2026-11-06, the principal offence of communicating a false statement of fact in Singapore is created by section 7 of the Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act 2019 (POFMA), and it applies only where a number of specific elements are present. [CITE:4]

## 1. The core offence under section 7

A person must not do any act, whether in or outside Singapore, in order to communicate in Singapore a statement where the person knows or has reason to believe both that the statement is false and that communicating it in Singapore is likely to prejudice one of six listed interests. [CITE:4] The elements can be broken down as follows.

**Act done to communicate in Singapore.** The prohibition covers acts done inside or outside Singapore where the object is that a statement be communicated in Singapore. [CITE:4]

**A "statement of fact".** A statement of fact is one which a reasonable person seeing, hearing or otherwise perceiving it would consider to be a representation of fact. [CITE:15]

**The statement must be false.** A statement is false if it is false or misleading, whether wholly or in part, and whether on its own or in the context in which it appears. [CITE:15]

**The required state of mind.** The person must know, or have reason to believe, both that the statement is a false statement of fact and that communicating it in Singapore is likely to cause one of the listed harms. [CITE:4]

**The communication must be likely to prejudice at least one of six interests:**
- the security of Singapore or any part of Singapore;
- public health, public safety, public tranquillity or public finances;
- the friendly relations of Singapore with other countries;
- the outcome of an election to the office of President, a general election of Members of Parliament, a by-election of Members of Parliament, or a referendum;
- incitement of feelings of enmity, hatred or ill-will between different groups of persons; or
- diminishing public confidence in the performance of any duty or function of, or the exercise of any power by, the Government, an Organ of State, a statutory board, or part of any of them. [CITE:4]

**Meaning of "communicated in Singapore".** For Part 2 offences, a statement is communicated in Singapore if it is made available to one or more end-users in Singapore on or through the internet, or through MMS or SMS, and communicating includes causing its communication in Singapore. [CITE:18]

A false statement that does not satisfy these elements is not, by itself, an offence under section 7. [CITE:4] The Act's stated purposes include preventing the communication of false statements of fact in Singapore and enabling measures to counteract the effects of such communication. [CITE:8]

## 2. Penalties

**Ordinary penalties.** On conviction, an individual is liable to a fine not exceeding $50,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 5 years or to both; in any other case, the maximum is a fine not exceeding $500,000. [CITE:4]

**Higher penalties where an inauthentic online account or a bot is used.** Where such an account or bot is used to communicate the statement and for the purpose of accelerating that communication, an individual is liable to a fine not exceeding $100,000 or imprisonment not exceeding 10 years or both, and in any other case to a fine not exceeding $1 million. [CITE:4]

## 3. Statutory carve-out from section 7

Section 7 does not apply to any act done for the purpose of, or incidental to, the provision of an internet intermediary service, a telecommunication service, a service giving the public access to the internet, or a computing resource service. [CITE:4] Similar carve-outs appear in the related offences dealing with bots and service providers. [CITE:7] [CITE:3]

## 4. Closely related offences

**Making or altering bots (section 8).** It is an offence, whether in or outside Singapore, to make or alter a bot with the intention of communicating a false statement of fact in Singapore by means of the bot, or of enabling another person to do so; penalties are a fine not exceeding $30,000 or imprisonment not exceeding 3 years or both for an individual, and a fine not exceeding $500,000 otherwise, rising to a fine not exceeding $60,000 or imprisonment not exceeding 6 years or both for an individual, and a fine not exceeding $1 million otherwise, where the communication is likely to cause one of the listed harms. [CITE:7]

**Providing services for communication of false statements (section 9).** It is an offence to solicit, receive or agree to receive any financial or other material benefit as an inducement or reward for providing a service, knowing that the service is or will be used to communicate one or more false statements of fact in Singapore, where the service is in fact so used; penalties are a fine not exceeding $30,000 or imprisonment not exceeding 3 years or both for an individual and a fine not exceeding $500,000 otherwise, with higher penalties (a fine not exceeding $60,000 or imprisonment not exceeding 6 years or both; or a fine not exceeding $1 million) where the communication is likely to cause one of the listed harms. [CITE:3] Section 9(4) excludes acts for the purpose of, or incidental to, provision of the four types of services listed above, and on conviction the court must also order the person to pay a penalty equal to the financial or other material benefit received, although the supplied extract of section 9(5) is truncated. [CITE:3]

**Paid content (section 47).** A prescribed digital advertising intermediary or prescribed internet intermediary must take reasonable steps, in and outside Singapore, to ensure it does not facilitate communication in Singapore of paid content giving publicity to, or otherwise promoting, an online location that includes the subject statement of a Part 3 or Part 4 Direction; contravention is an offence punishable by a fine not exceeding $20,000 or imprisonment not exceeding 12 months or both for an individual, and a fine not exceeding $500,000 otherwise. [CITE:11]

## 5. Part 3 Directions are separate from the communication offence

A false statement of fact that is being communicated in Singapore may also be dealt with through the direction regime, which operates alongside the criminal offences. [CITE:20]

**Issuance.** A Minister may instruct the Competent Authority to issue a Part 3 Direction if a false statement of fact has been or is being communicated in Singapore and the Minister is of the opinion that it is in the public interest to issue it, and a Direction may be issued even if the statement has been amended or has ceased to be communicated in Singapore. [CITE:20]

**Service.** A Part 3 Direction may be served by prescribed means, including electronic means, on the person to whom it is issued or on a person in Singapore whom that person has appointed to accept service on their behalf. [CITE:6]

**Non-compliance is a separate offence (section 15).** A person to whom a Direction is issued and served who, without reasonable excuse, fails to comply with it, whether in or outside Singapore, is guilty of an offence: for an individual, a fine not exceeding $20,000 or imprisonment not exceeding 12 months or both; in any other case, a fine not exceeding $500,000. [CITE:2] It is not a defence that another written law, rule of law, contract or professional conduct rule prevents or restricts compliance, nor that the person has applied to vary or cancel the Direction under section 19 or appealed to the General Division of the High Court. [CITE:2] However, no civil or criminal liability is incurred by the person or its officers, employees or agents for acts or omissions done with reasonable care and in good faith for the purpose of complying with the Direction. [CITE:2]

**Access blocking (section 16).** Where a person fails to comply with a Part 3 Direction, the subject statement is being communicated in Singapore on an online location, and the Minister is satisfied that end-users in Singapore have used or are using the services of an internet access service provider to access that location, the Minister may direct IMDA to order the provider to take reasonable steps to disable access, and IMDA must do so. [CITE:5] An internet access service provider that does not comply is guilty of an offence, liable to a fine not exceeding $20,000 for each day of non-compliance up to $500,000. [CITE:5]

**Appeal.** A person to whom a Direction is issued may appeal to the General Division of the High Court, but only after first applying to the Minister to vary or cancel the Direction and being refused; the Direction remains in effect during the appeal unless set aside, although a stay may be granted where a prima facie case of technical impossibility is established. [CITE:9] The grounds on which the court may set aside a Direction are limited to whether the person communicated the subject statement in Singapore, whether the subject statement is a statement of fact or is true, and whether it is technically impossible to comply. [CITE:9]

**Other causes of action preserved.** Issuing a Part 3 Direction does not affect any power or right of any person, including a Minister, the Competent Authority or the Government, to take any other action under the Act or any other law in relation to the statement, or the Public Prosecutor's power to initiate proceedings for an offence. [CITE:1] The equivalent preservation applies to Directions concerning inauthentic online accounts under Part 6. [CITE:17] Where an internet intermediary fails to comply with an Account Restriction Direction, the Minister may also direct IMDA to order an internet access service provider to take reasonable steps to disable access to the relevant online location. [CITE:13] [CITE:14]

## 6. Who may be liable, and jurisdiction

**Corporations (section 58).** Where a corporation commits a Part 2 offence, a person who is an officer, or an individual involved in the management of the corporation and in a position to influence its conduct in relation to the offence, commits the same offence if the person consented or connived or conspired to effect the offence, was knowingly concerned in or a party to its commission, or knew or ought reasonably to have known that the offence was being committed and failed to take all reasonable steps to prevent or stop it. [CITE:12] Evidence that an officer, employee or agent engaged in the conduct within the scope of their actual or apparent authority and had the relevant state of mind is evidence that the corporation had that state of mind. [CITE:12]

**Unincorporated associations and partnerships (section 59).** The same attribution and individual-liability rules apply to unincorporated associations and partnerships, including their officers, governing body members, partners and certain managers. [CITE:19]

**Offences committed outside Singapore (section 60).** Where an offence under sections 7, 8, 9, 15, 27, 32(6), 34(5), 36, 37, 38, 42, 47 or 50(3) is committed by a person outside Singapore, the person may be dealt with with respect to that offence as if it had been committed within Singapore. [CITE:10] Despite the Criminal Procedure Code 2010, a District Court or a Magistrate's Court has jurisdiction to try any offence under the Act and may impose the full punishment for it. [CITE:10]

**Compounding (section 57).** An authorised officer authorised in writing by the Minister may compound any offence prescribed as compoundable by collecting from a person reasonably suspected of the offence a sum not exceeding one half of the maximum fine prescribed for that offence, after which no further proceedings may be taken against that person in respect of it. [CITE:16]

## 7. Note on the currency of these provisions

The supplied sections are drawn from the published 2020 Edition of POFMA as reproduced on Singapore Statutes Online, with some extracts reflecting amendments current to 31 December 2021, and each source directs readers to check Singapore Statutes Online for the latest version. [CITE:4] [CITE:15]

I could not find strong authority in the sources provided for the full text of the Montreal Convention's own complaint provision (Article 31): the source for section 8 of the 2007 Act explains only how "damage" and "receipt" are construed in paragraph 2 of Article 31 and does not reproduce that paragraph's time limits [CITE:3]. The answer below therefore rests on the Singapore statutory provisions that directly address partial loss.

**As at 2026-11-06, the short answer is yes: the complaint rule for damaged baggage also covers baggage that is only partly lost.**

**What the Singapore statutes say**

- For international carriage governed by the Montreal Convention 1999, references to "damage" in paragraph 2 of Article 31 are construed as including loss of part of the baggage or cargo in question [CITE:3].
- The Carriage by Air Act 1988 makes the same construction for Article 26(2) in its First, Second and Third Schedules: references to "damage" include loss of part of the baggage or cargo, and references to receipt are construed as receipt of the remainder [CITE:2].
- For working out when the complaint period runs, receipt of baggage or cargo in a partial-loss case is therefore treated as receipt of the remainder of it, rather than receipt of the missing items [CITE:3][CITE:2].
- The Montreal Convention applies to all international carriage of persons, baggage or cargo performed by aircraft for reward, and equally to gratuitous carriage by an air transport undertaking [CITE:10]. "International carriage" means carriage between two States Parties, or within one State Party where there is an agreed stopping place in another State; carriage between two points in one State Party with no such agreed stopping place is not international carriage for the Convention's purposes [CITE:10].

**Time limits and form of complaint**

- Under the Second Schedule to the Carriage by Air Act 1988, the person entitled to delivery must complain to the carrier forthwith after discovering the damage and, at the latest, within three days from the date of receipt for baggage, seven days for cargo, and fourteen days from the date the baggage or cargo was placed at that person's disposal in the case of delay [CITE:1].
- Every complaint must be made in writing on the document of carriage or by a separate written notice despatched within those times, and if no complaint is made within them, no action lies against the carrier unless the carrier was fraudulent [CITE:1].
- The precise deadlines in paragraph 2 of Article 31 of the Montreal Convention are not set out in the sources provided; section 8 of the 2007 Act only governs how "damage" and "receipt" are read in that paragraph [CITE:3]. The time limits themselves appear in Article 31 of the Convention as scheduled in the 2007 Act, which is available on Singapore Statutes Online [CITE:10].

**Other time limits that the same sources report**

- Under the Carriage by Air Act 1988 Schedules, the right to damages is extinguished if an action is not brought within two years, reckoned from the date of arrival at the destination, the date the aircraft ought to have arrived, or the date the carriage stopped, with the method of calculation governed by the law of the court hearing the case [CITE:8][CITE:1].

**Liability limits, if a claim is pursued**

- Where the loss concerns part of registered baggage or cargo, the weight taken into account for the carrier's liability limit is the total weight of the package or packages concerned [CITE:15].
- The revised Montreal limits, with effect from 28 December 2024, are 1,519 Special Drawing Rights per passenger for destruction, loss, damage or delay of baggage, and 26 Special Drawing Rights per kilogram for cargo [CITE:7].

**Scope limits of this answer**

- If the items were damaged or lost on the ground at an airport rather than missing from checked baggage, the air-carriage complaint rules above would not be the operative framework: section 42 of the Air Navigation Act 1966 makes the owner of an aircraft liable for material damage or loss caused by an aircraft in flight, taking off or landing, without proof of negligence, and the duty-of-care and pure-economic-loss analysis in NTUC Foodfare Co-operative Ltd v SIA Engineering Company Limited [2017] SGHC 250 would be a separate route [CITE:13][CITE:14][CITE:16].
- The sources provided do not set out the Montreal Article 31 deadlines or the current full text of the Carriage by Air Act 1988; the latest consolidated versions should be checked on Singapore Statutes Online, or with a lawyer.

**As at 2026-11-06, yes.** Singapore customs officers have a statutory power to open a parcel sent to you from overseas, and under the main customs power they do not need your consent to do so.

### The general customs power

Section 108 of the Customs Act 1960 provides that any proper officer of customs may examine goods in the course of being imported or exported or intended to be imported or exported, direct goods to be brought to a customs office or customs station, and open any package or receptacle [CITE:1]. A parcel posted to you from overseas is goods intended to be imported, so this is the principal provision under which it can be opened [CITE:1]. The excerpt of the Customs Act's interpretation section supplied does not define the term "proper officer of customs" [CITE:20].

Separately, where you arrive from overseas, section 109 requires a person landing or having recently landed from a vessel or aircraft, or entering or having recently entered Singapore by road or rail, on demand to permit their person, goods and baggage to be searched [CITE:12]. If you ask to be present when your goods and baggage are searched and do so within a reasonable time, they may not be searched except in your presence [CITE:12].

For cargo arriving by sea or air, a proper officer of customs may board a vessel or aircraft, rummage and search all parts of it, examine all goods on board, and open any locked place, box or chest if the key is withheld [CITE:8]. Goods or packages lodged in a Government warehouse, licensed warehouse, customs office or customs station may be ordered to be opened, weighed or otherwise examined by a senior officer of customs [CITE:2].

### Schemes with a suspicion threshold

Some border powers apply only where there is a reasonable suspicion that the item contains goods liable to seizure. Under the Trade Marks Act 1998, goods, packages or other articles being imported, recently imported or being exported may be examined and searched where a reasonable suspicion exists that they contain goods liable to seizure under section 82 or 93A, and a senior authorised officer may forcibly open the article, with the person in charge afforded every reasonable facility to be present [CITE:16]. The Copyright Act 2021 applies a similar framework, and makes it an offence for a person other than a customs officer to remove, open, break or tamper with a mark, lock or seal applied under that power, punishable by a fine of up to $6,000, imprisonment of up to 6 months, or both [CITE:6]. The Geographical Indications Act 2014 contains comparable examination, detention, forcible-opening and seal-tampering provisions [CITE:9].

On a different footing, a senior officer of customs, a police officer of at least sergeant rank, a postal licensee officer of at least postal superintendent rank, or a person authorised by the Minister may detain, open and examine any package suspected to contain a prohibited publication [CITE:19]. The same applies to packages suspected to contain a declared foreign newspaper, which may be impounded and delivered to the Registrar [CITE:7].

### If the parcel went to a public parcel locker

Where the Postal Authority knows or has reason to suspect that a parcel in a public parcel locker may be the subject of an offence under the Postal Services Act or its regulations, it may direct the locker network operator in writing to open and search lockers and to detain and open parcels [CITE:5]. Separately, a person who is not the intended recipient and who wilfully retains, secretes or opens such a parcel commits an offence, unless the Postal Authority authorises it, the intended recipient authorises it, or the parent-or-guardian exception for a minor or ward applies [CITE:3]. Staff of the locker network operator and delivery service providers, including officers, employees, agents and contractors, commit offences for wilfully opening parcels contrary to their duty, destroying or throwing away parcels, and removing identifying marks [CITE:14].

### After seizure, sampling, and cost

Once goods suspected of being uncustomed or otherwise liable to seizure have been seized, it is sufficient for a proper officer of customs to open, examine and if necessary test the contents of such proportion of the seized goods as the officer determines, and the court is to presume that goods in the unopened packages are of the same nature, quantity and quality as those found in the packages opened [CITE:10].

The Customs Act places the cost of operations such as opening, unpacking and repacking on the owner, importer, exporter, consignor, consignee or agent, as the case may be [CITE:15]. The Customs Act text quoted is the consolidated version stated to be in force from 1 July 2025, and the source itself notes that Singapore Statutes Online should be checked for the latest version [CITE:1].

### Two points of distinction

The powers in the States of Malaya Customs Duties Collection Act 1958 on opening packages and examining 10% of seized packages concern "Federal officer of customs" and goods exported from or intended to be imported into Malaysia, so they describe Malaysian law rather than Singapore's [CITE:4] [CITE:13].

Consular bags are dealt with separately under the Second Schedule to the Diplomatic and Consular Relations Act 2005, which allows a consular bag to be entrusted to the captain of a ship or commercial aircraft with an official document indicating the number of packages, and provides that the immunities in paragraph 5 continue to apply to an ad hoc consular courier until the bag has been delivered to the consignee; the extract supplied does not set out paragraph 5 itself [CITE:17].

## 1. The information sharing arrangement (s 23(1))

A licensee providing a shared mobility service may enter into an information sharing arrangement with another licensee providing a shared mobility service, using the same or a different type of vehicles, to share or exchange information they hold for the purposes of s 23(4). [CITE:1] Section 23 operates between licensees; a class licensee is not a party to such an arrangement under s 23, although LTA directions under s 25 may be addressed to a class licensee as well as a licensee. [CITE:1][CITE:5]

## 2. What may be shared, and the limits on sharing (s 23(2)–(3))

Each party to the arrangement is authorised, despite any other Act, to request and receive information held by the other party and to disclose information to it, but only to the extent that the information is reasonably necessary to assist in exercising a power under s 23(4). [CITE:1] The information that may be exchanged is confined to three categories: information concerning possible improper parking in public places by hirers of vehicles hired from licensees who are parties to the arrangement; information about hirers in respect of whom a power under s 23(4) has been exercised by any party to the arrangement; and other information prescribed by regulations. [CITE:1]

## 3. What the shared information is used for (s 23(4)–(5))

Every licensee is entitled to refuse to hire, or further hire, an individual any undocked vehicle it uses to provide the service, for a period not exceeding a prescribed period, where the licensee has reasonable grounds to believe that the individual persistently improperly parks vehicles in public places, whether or not those vehicles were hired from the same licensee. [CITE:1] A licensee must refuse to hire or further hire a particular individual where the LTA has directed it to do so under s 25. [CITE:1] The term "undocked" is used in the Act in relation to allowing a hiring to end with the vehicle left in a public place rather than returned to a docking point. [CITE:2]

For the persistent-parking ground, an individual seeking to hire an undocked vehicle may be treated as a persistent improper parker if, pursuant to an information sharing arrangement, the licensee reasonably believes that the individual, upon ending a hiring from that licensee or another licensee, improperly parked a vehicle in a public place on at least 3 earlier occasions within the year. [CITE:1] Note the asymmetry in the two limbs: refusal based on persistent improper parking is a right ("is entitled to refuse"), whereas refusal following an LTA direction is a duty ("must refuse"). [CITE:1]

## 4. Limits on LTA directions to refuse hiring (s 25)

The LTA may direct a licensee or class licensee to do or refrain from doing specified things for a specified period, including refusing to hire or further hire vehicles to a particular hirer, and may revoke the direction at any time. [CITE:5] A direction requiring refusal to hire may only be made in respect of an individual who has been convicted of, or has accepted a composition sum offered in respect of, specified offences — including offences under the Parking Places Act 1974 or rules under that Act involving improper parking of vehicles hired from any licensee or class licensee — committed or allegedly committed on or after 22 July 2020. [CITE:5] Such a direction cannot have an expiry date longer than the prescribed period mentioned in s 23(4)(b), and it continues in force until the earlier of the expiry date stated in it or the LTA's revocation of it. [CITE:5]

## 5. Related but separate regimes

Record-keeping and information-giving to the LTA are dealt with separately in s 22, which requires licensees to keep and retain prescribed records and give information to the LTA, and creates offences for intentional or negligent contravention of those requirements, deliberate alteration, suppression or destruction of required records, and false statements made knowingly or recklessly. [CITE:13] The LTA may also issue or approve standards of performance on measures to discourage indiscriminate parking by hirers in public places at the end of hiring, which may include pricing measures and the use of geo-fencing technology. [CITE:16] On written notice, the LTA or an authorised officer may require a licensee or class licensee to provide documents and information relating to matters the authorised officer considers necessary for the purposes of s 32, so long as they are within the licensee's knowledge, custody or control, and the LTA may keep any document or information provided without payment. [CITE:6] Nothing in the Act limits the application of the Parking Places Act 1974 or any other written law to the parking of vehicles in public places, or affects the operation of the Active Mobility Act 2017 or the Road Traffic Act 1961. [CITE:14]

## 6. Points the supplied sources do not settle

The maximum period for refusal under s 23(4), and any additional categories of shareable information, are to be "prescribed", meaning set out in subsidiary regulations which the LTA may make, with the Minister's approval, to carry out or give effect to the Act. [CITE:1][CITE:7] The prescribed periods themselves are not in the supplied extracts, so their length cannot be stated from them; they would be found in the regulations made under s 48. [CITE:7] The supplied extracts are from the 2020 Edition as at 31 December 2021, and each records that the Singapore Statutes Online version should be checked for the latest text. [CITE:1][CITE:2][CITE:5][CITE:7]

As at 2026-11-06, I could not find strong case-law authority in the supplied sources for quantifying fault on these particular facts; the directly applicable statutory rule is nevertheless clear. [CITE:2]

For collision-related damage or loss to a ship, cargo, freight, or other property aboard, where two or more ships are at fault, each ship’s liability to make good the loss is proportionate to the degree of that ship’s fault. [CITE:2] If different degrees of fault cannot be established, the liability is apportioned equally. [CITE:2] A ship is not liable for loss or damage to which its own fault did not contribute. [CITE:2]

Accordingly, the split is not automatically 50/50 merely because both ships contributed to the collision; it follows their respective degrees of fault, unless those degrees cannot be distinguished. [CITE:2] Assessing relative fault is fact-sensitive and takes account of the parties’ blameworthiness in light of the causal effect of their conduct. [CITE:18]

If the loss is death or personal injury suffered by someone aboard, the shipowners’ liability is instead joint and several, meaning each may be responsible for the full recoverable loss. [CITE:7] An owner who pays more than its ship’s proper share may recover the excess by contribution from the other owner or owners according to their respective fault. [CITE:14]

As at 2026-11-06, under section 6(1) of the Maritime Conventions Act 1911, a ship’s master or person in charge must, so far as possible without serious danger to their own ship, crew and passengers, render assistance to every person found at sea in danger of being lost—including a person from a foreign state at war with Singapore. Failure to do so is an offence. [CITE:1]

The master’s compliance with this duty does not affect their own right, or any other person’s right, to salvage. [CITE:1]

**As at 2026-11-06, under Singapore's Maritime Conventions Act 1911, the time limit for bringing an action of this kind is two years.**

### The main rule

Section 8(1) provides that no action is maintainable to enforce any claim or lien against a ship or her owners in respect of, among other things, damage or loss to another ship, her cargo or freight, or any property on board her, or damages for loss of life or personal injuries suffered by any person on board her, caused by the fault of the former ship, whether that ship is wholly or partly in fault, unless proceedings are commenced within two years from the date when the damage, loss or injury was caused. [CITE:1]

For damage caused to another ship by the fault of the defendant ship, the clock therefore runs from the date the damage was caused, and the claim becomes barred if proceedings are not commenced within two years of that date. [CITE:1] The Singapore High Court has described section 8(1) in the same way when explaining the time bar defence in *See Toh Siew Kee v Ho Ah Lam Ferrocement (Pte) Ltd and others* [2012] SGHC 87. [CITE:9]

### Court power to extend the period

The two-year period is not absolute. Under section 8(3)(a), a court with jurisdiction to deal with such an action may, in accordance with the Rules of Court, extend the period to such extent and on such conditions as it thinks fit. [CITE:1] Under section 8(3)(b), the court **must** extend the period, to an extent sufficient to give a reasonable opportunity, if it is satisfied that during the period there was no reasonable opportunity of arresting the defendant ship within the jurisdiction of the court, or within the territorial waters of the country to which the plaintiff's ship belongs or in which the plaintiff resides or has his principal place of business. [CITE:1]

### Related points

- A different, shorter period applies to a claim for contribution in respect of an overpaid proportion of damages for loss of life or personal injuries: proceedings must be commenced within one year from the date of payment. [CITE:1]
- Where, by virtue of a charter or demise or for any other reason, the owners are not responsible for the navigation and management of the ship, the Act is read as though references to owners were substituted with references to the charterers or other persons for the time being so responsible. [CITE:5]
- The Act was declared by the Application of English Law Act 1993 to apply or continue to apply in Singapore, and it is construed as one with the Merchant Shipping Act 1995. [CITE:10]

As at 2026-11-06, on the supplied statutory texts, section 5 of the Tokyo Convention Act 1971 sets the following conditions and limits for action by an aircraft’s commander against a person on board. [CITE:1]

### Statutory threshold

Section 5(2) applies to the commander of an aircraft in flight, wherever the aircraft may be. [CITE:1] The commander has reasonable grounds to believe, in respect of a person on board, either:

- that the person has done, or is about to do while the aircraft is in flight, an act that jeopardises or may jeopardise the safety of the aircraft, persons or property on board, or good order and discipline on board; or
- that the person has done an act on board while the aircraft is in flight which, in the commander’s opinion, is a serious offence. [CITE:1]

Subject to section 5(7), once either threshold is met, the commander may take reasonable measures, including restraint of the person, as necessary to protect the safety of the aircraft or persons or property on board, maintain good order and discipline on board, or enable the person’s disembarkation or delivery in accordance with section 5(8). [CITE:1]

The commander may require a crew member to assist in restraining such a person, or request—but not require—a passenger or air marshal to provide that assistance. [CITE:1]

### Disembarkation and delivery

Where the commander has the safety or good-order grounds described in section 5(2)(a), and believes disembarkation is necessary to protect safety or maintain good order and discipline, the commander may disembark the person in any country in which the aircraft may be. [CITE:2]

Where the commander has the serious-offence grounds described in section 5(2)(b), the commander may deliver the person in Singapore to a police officer or immigration officer, or in another Convention country to an officer performing corresponding functions. [CITE:2]

The commander must report a qualifying disembarkation, and the reasons for it, to the appropriate authority in the country of disembarkation and the appropriate diplomatic or consular office of the person’s country of nationality. [CITE:2] For an intended delivery, the commander must notify the relevant local authority and the person’s diplomatic or consular office before, or as soon as reasonably practicable after, landing; failure without reasonable cause is an offence punishable by a fine not exceeding $1,000. [CITE:2]

### Limits and protection from liability

Except for protecting the safety of the aircraft or persons or property on board, the Act does not authorise action concerning a political offence or an offence based on discrimination such as race, religion, nationality, ethnic origin, political opinion or gender. [CITE:8]

No liability lies against the commander, crew member, passenger, air marshal, owner or operator, or person on whose behalf the flight was performed, on account of treatment undergone by a person against whom action was taken under the Act. [CITE:3]

One qualification remains: section 5(2) expressly makes the commander’s power subject to section 5(7), but the supplied excerpts do not reproduce section 5(7), so its additional requirements cannot be stated from these sources. [CITE:1] The omitted qualification can be checked in the current Singapore Statutes Online text of section 5 or with a Singapore lawyer. [CITE:1]

“Unlawfully” means, for an act committed in Singapore, that the act constitutes an offence apart from this Act under Singapore law; for an act committed outside Singapore, it means that the act would have constituted such an offence if committed in Singapore. [CITE:17]

As at 2026-11-06, **yes — but only within the statutory limits set out below.** The power belongs to a "public telecommunication licensee", the statutory term used in the Act for the utility exercising these powers. [CITE:1]

## The statutory test

Section 22(1) of the Telecommunications Act 1999 provides that, where in the opinion of the public telecommunication licensee there is danger or suspected danger that any tree near its installation or plant may interrupt or interfere with any telecommunication service provided by the licensee, or cause damage to that installation or plant, the licensee may cause the tree to be felled or dealt with in another manner that will, in its opinion, avert the danger. [CITE:1]

The trigger is "danger or suspected danger" rather than proof that damage has already occurred, and the power is discretionary ("may"). [CITE:1] For this section, "tree" includes undergrowth, so the power extends to vegetation growing beneath the tree. [CITE:1]

Unlike the railway legislation, which requires the permission of a Magistrate's Court before a tree near a railway may be felled except in an emergency, the telecommunications, electricity and gas provisions contain no such court-permission requirement. [CITE:13][CITE:1][CITE:5][CITE:7]

## Limits imposed by the Parks and Trees Act 2005

A licensee exercising the section 22 power is subject to the Parks and Trees Act 2005. [CITE:1] On that basis:

- A tree with a girth exceeding one metre growing on a tree conservation area or on vacant land must not be cut except with the Commissioner's approval under section 20 and in accordance with its terms; contravention is an offence punishable by a fine of up to $50,000, and no approval is needed where the condition of the tree constitutes an immediate threat to life or property. [CITE:4]
- Within a heritage road green buffer, no tree or plant may be cut or damaged without the Commissioner's approval; that is an offence punishable by a fine of up to $50,000, and approval is not required where the Commissioner determines the tree or plant is dying or dead, or its condition constitutes an immediate threat to life or property. [CITE:8]
- Within a national park or nature reserve, cutting, collecting or displacing any tree or plant requires the Commissioner's approval under section 12; contravention is an offence carrying a fine of up to $50,000, imprisonment of up to 6 months, or both, plus a continuing fine of $500 for each day or part of a day after conviction. [CITE:18]
- Where the Commissioner is satisfied that a tree or plant constitutes an immediate threat to life or property, or that it is reasonably necessary to cut or damage it to protect life or property from fire, the Commissioner may carry out the cutting and the resulting costs and expenses are recoverable from the occupier as a debt. [CITE:9]
- In proceedings for offences under section 14, section 18 or section 27, it is presumed (until the contrary is proved) that the occupier, or where building works were being carried out, the person doing the works, the employer, and the person who instructed or permitted the cutting or damage, cut or damaged the tree or plant. [CITE:6]

## Compensation for the felled tree

Where the tree existed before the licensee's installation or plant was placed, erected or installed, the licensee may, subject to subsections (4) and (5), pay any person adversely affected "such sum as may be agreed by way of compensation". [CITE:1] The wording differs from the comparable electricity and gas provisions, which use mandatory wording ("must … pay") and, for electricity, allow the Authority to determine the sum if agreement is not reached. [CITE:5][CITE:7]

No further compensation is payable for felling, lopping or clearing where the work is necessary for maintenance of the installation or plant and the tree or vegetation has grown, or been allowed to grow, since compensation was previously paid. [CITE:1] No compensation is payable for a tree within 20 metres of the centre line of any road constructed or maintained by the Government or a public authority unless it is proved that the tree existed before the road was constructed. [CITE:1]

## The owner's or occupier's own obligations

If the owner or occupier of land fells, lops or clears a tree or vegetation adjacent to the licensee's installation or plant, they must give the licensee 14 days' written notice of the intention and take all such reasonable precautions as the licensee requires to protect the installation or plant. [CITE:1] If the owner or occupier fails to give that notice, or fails to take the required precautions after notice, they are liable to pay the licensee the cost and expense incurred for any damage caused to the installation or plant. [CITE:1]

## Related entry and maintenance powers

- For inspecting, maintaining or repairing its installation or plant, the licensee or a person it authorises may enter any land or building at a reasonable time, whether or not the installation or plant is on it, and may in that course fell or lop trees and remove vegetation, causing as little damage as possible, and pay compensation for damage for which compensation has not already been assessed under section 17. [CITE:2]
- For preparatory works on land other than State land, the licensee must give the occupier at least 3 hours' previous notice, and this power does not authorise cutting down or clearing vegetation, nor entering any building or an enclosure attached to a building. [CITE:3]
- On State land, the licensee may enter at a reasonable time and may, in the course of the works, fell or lop trees and remove vegetation, and must pay compensation for damage or disturbance to improvements, buildings, growing trees or crops. [CITE:14]

## Proving loss is a separate question

Compensation or damages claims are distinct from the power to fell. In *NTUC Foodfare Co-operative Ltd v SIA Engineering Company Limited & Anor*, the General Division of the High Court observed that a concern about safety did not in itself prove that a kiosk was damaged or unsafe, and found no evidence of damage on the facts before it. [CITE:20]

**As at 2026-11-06, yes — a shop may sell goods to the public inside a free trade zone, but only with the written authorisation of the zone's licensed FTZ operator and on such conditions as that operator imposes.** [CITE:2]

## 1. The basic rule: retail trade needs written authorisation

Section 8(1) of the Free Trade Zones Act 1966 provides that no retail trade shall be conducted within a free trade zone unless it is authorised in writing by the licensed FTZ operator of the zone and is subject to such conditions as the operator may impose. [CITE:2] Selling goods to the public in the zone is the kind of activity that this retail trade provision governs, and section 5(2)(b) lists "sold" among the operations permitted on goods in a free trade zone. [CITE:1]

For this purpose, a "free trade zone" means an area declared to be one under section 3(1), an "FTZ operator" is the person who administers, maintains and operates it, a "licensed FTZ operator" is one holding a valid FTZ operator licence, and "customs territory" means Singapore and its territorial waters but excluding any free trade zone. [CITE:18]

The operator's authorisation is also constrained by its own general powers: goods in the zone may be stored, sold, exhibited, repacked, assembled, distributed and otherwise manipulated only "unless otherwise directed by the licensed FTZ operator", so the operator can direct that a particular operation, including sale, is not to be carried out. [CITE:1] After each retail trade authorisation, the licensed FTZ operator must submit to the Director-General of Customs the prescribed information and documents about the authorisation within the prescribed period. [CITE:2]

## 2. Duty and tax on goods sold

Section 9 provides that, subject to sections 5, 6 and 8, a person who knows or has reason to believe that customs duty or tax on any dutiable goods or taxable goods in a free trade zone has not been paid to the Director-General must not use or consume those goods unless the duty and tax are paid before the use or consumption. [CITE:4] "Dutiable goods" means goods subject to customs duty on entry into customs territory, or manufactured in Singapore including in a free trade zone, on which duty has not been paid, and includes goods manufactured in a free trade zone from materials of a class dutiable on entry into customs territory for consumption there. [CITE:18]

The statutory wording addresses "use or consume", and the provided sources do not define those words or state expressly whether a retail sale falls within them. [CITE:4][CITE:18]

The Customs Act also allocates liability for duty on goods that stay in the zone. Dutiable goods unshipped or landed in a free trade zone remain at the risk of the master, owner or agent of the vessel, the pilot, owner or agent of the aircraft, or a person authorised under section 39(2), until they are lawfully removed for export or entry into customs territory, or are received for storage by the licensed FTZ operator or the occupier or operator of the premises where the goods are stored within the zone. [CITE:12] Where dutiable goods are received for storage by the licensed FTZ operator or the occupier or operator of the premises, that person is liable to pay customs duty or excise duty on goods not accounted for to the satisfaction of a senior officer of customs, as if the goods had been imported. [CITE:12] Where dutiable goods landed in a free trade zone are used or consumed in the zone, the relevant persons at whose risk the goods remained, and the licensed FTZ operator, occupier or operator where the goods were stored by them, are liable to pay customs duty or excise duty on the goods so used or consumed, as if the goods had been imported. [CITE:12]

Goods of a class dutiable on entry into customs territory that are sent from a free trade zone into the customs territory are subject to the Customs Act 1960, and goods brought into a free trade zone from customs territory are deemed exported for the purpose of drawback under that Act unless the Minister has prescribed otherwise. [CITE:1] For goods lawfully brought into or manufactured in a free trade zone, the applicable customs duty rate and valuation are fixed by reference to specified dates, such as the day the goods are sent into the customs territory where no manipulation or manufacture effected a change in tariff classification. [CITE:11]

## 3. Activities beyond simple retail sale

Any manufacture of goods in a free trade zone requires written notice of the intention and the Director-General's prior written permission, and assembling, mixing or otherwise manipulating dutiable goods for entry into the customs territory requires the same notice and permission. [CITE:5] That permission may be granted or withheld in the Director-General's discretion, and permitted manipulation or manufacture is subject to regulations made under the Act and to conditions the Director-General may impose. [CITE:5]

Where the Director-General gives an allowance for recoverable and irrecoverable waste, recoverable waste sent into the customs territory is subject to customs duty and tax in its condition, quantity and weight at the time of entry. [CITE:5]

## 4. Operator and Director-General orders affecting the shop

The licensed FTZ operator may, by written order, prohibit a person from bringing goods into the zone or require their removal, and may require the discontinuance of operations, where the goods or operations are dangerous or prejudicial to the public interest, health or safety. [CITE:3] The Director-General may make the same orders where, in the Director-General's opinion, the goods or operations are dangerous or prejudicial to the public interest, health or safety. [CITE:3] Failure to comply with an order is an offence punishable by a fine not exceeding $10,000, and the Director-General may enter the zone and take the measures and do the work necessary to give effect to the order, recovering the costs as a debt due to the Government from the person who failed to comply. [CITE:3]

The licensed FTZ operator may also permit any person to erect buildings and other structures within the zone, subject to conditions the operator may impose, and such permission does not create a vested right against the operator or the Government. [CITE:13]

## 5. Penalties and enforcement

A contravention of section 8 is an offence punishable on conviction by a fine not exceeding $10,000. [CITE:19] A contravention of section 9 is an offence punishable on conviction by a fine not exceeding the greater of $10,000 or the sum total of the customs duty and tax on the goods concerned, or by imprisonment for a term not exceeding 12 months, or both. [CITE:19] Failure to comply with a direction given by the licensed FTZ operator under section 5(2), or failure to comply with section 6(1), is likewise an offence with the same maximum fine or imprisonment of up to 12 months, or both. [CITE:19]

Customs officers entering a free trade zone under section 14R have full and free access to the zone and may search it, examine activities and operations, take photographs and recordings, carry out inspections, audits and stock checks, require information and documents, inspect goods, documents and computers, and take possession of items where necessary for inspection or as evidence of a contravention. [CITE:7] The Director-General may also direct an FTZ cargo handler to detain goods suspected to be involved in an offence for inspection, with the inspection ordinarily to be completed within 48 hours of access unless the Director-General certifies that the nature, quantity or complexity of the goods or inspection makes that impossible. [CITE:9]

## 6. Points the provided sources do not resolve

The excerpt of the interpretation section does not define "retail trade", so the precise boundary of the section 8 authorisation requirement for particular selling models is not settled by the material supplied. [CITE:18][CITE:2] The prescribed period and the prescribed information and documents for the section 8(2) return are not set out in these excerpts and would need to be checked in the subsidiary legislation made under the Act. [CITE:2][CITE:5] The sources themselves note that the published copies are consolidated versions and that Singapore Statutes Online should be checked for the latest text. [CITE:2][CITE:6]

- The Minister may, in special cases, approve the enrolment of persons who are neither citizens of Singapore nor permanent residents of Singapore. [CITE:1]
